## Object defaults

### `withDefaults(defaults?, ...overrides)`

Performs a shallow merge of defaults and overrides into a new object, preserving earlier values when a property is missing or `undefined`.

Use it to supply default values without writing a separate fallback for each property. Pass defaults first, then override objects from left to right. A later defined value replaces the earlier value, including when it is `null`, `false`, `0` or an empty string. An `undefined` override keeps the most recent earlier value.

**Parameters**

| Parameter      | Type                              | Description                                                |
| -------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `defaults?`    | `object \| null \| undefined`     | Optional object containing the initial default values.     |
| `...overrides` | `(object \| null \| undefined)[]` | Zero or more override objects, applied from left to right. |

Arguments that are `null` or `undefined` are skipped in any position. With no arguments, the result is an empty object. Functions and other non-object arguments are rejected; function-valued properties are valid.

**Returns:** `Object` — A new plain object containing the combined properties. Nested objects and arrays retain their original references.

**Errors**

- `TypeError` if an argument is not an object, `null` or `undefined`. Rejected arguments are not coerced or invoked.
- Getter, proxy and reflection errors are passed through to the caller. Arguments are processed in order; after an error, later arguments are not read and earlier getter side effects are not undone.

**Examples**

Supply defaults for an undefined title while preserving explicit `false` and `0` values:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { title: 'Home', visible: true, count: 10 };
const overrides = { title: undefined, visible: false, count: 0 };

withDefaults(defaults, overrides);                     // => { title: 'Home', visible: false, count: 0 }
```

An undefined override keeps the most recent value, so it does not reset `count` to `10`:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { count: 10 };
const firstOverride = { count: 4 };
const lastOverride = { count: undefined };

withDefaults(defaults, firstOverride, lastOverride);   // => { count: 4 }
```

Without any defined properties to copy, the result is empty. Undefined-only properties are omitted:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

withDefaults();                                        // => {}
withDefaults(null, undefined);                         // => {}
withDefaults({ title: undefined });                    // => {}
```

**Notes**

#### Shallow copying

A nested override replaces the whole nested value. Its properties are not merged with those of the default, and neither object is cloned:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { appearance: { colour: 'blue', size: 'large' } };
const overrides = { appearance: { colour: 'red' } };
const result = withDefaults(defaults, overrides);

result;                                      // => { appearance: { colour: 'red' } }
result.appearance === overrides.appearance;  // => true
defaults.appearance;                         // => { colour: 'blue', size: 'large' }
```

#### Property copying

Only **own enumerable string and symbol properties** are copied. Inherited and non-enumerable properties are skipped. Symbols follow the same override rule:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const label = Symbol('label');
const defaults = { [label]: 'Home' };
const result = withDefaults(defaults, { [label]: undefined });

result[label];                                               // => 'Home'
```

For each source, the helper takes a snapshot of its own keys, then checks each property's current enumerability before reading it. Each eligible value is read once. A getter's defined return value becomes an ordinary writable, configurable, enumerable data property in the result; the getter itself is not copied. Getters and proxies can have side effects even though the helper does not assign to its sources.

Special names such as `__proto__` become own data properties without invoking inherited setters or changing the result's prototype:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const source = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"unexpected":true}}');
const result = withDefaults(source);

Object.getPrototypeOf(result) === Object.prototype;          // => true
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(result, '__proto__');   // => true
result.unexpected;                                           // => undefined
```

This protects the copying operation. The result can still contain values that are unsafe for a later operation, including another merge that handles `__proto__` differently.

#### Other object types

Plain data objects are the usual inputs. Other objects follow the same property-copying rules: arrays contribute enumerable indices, excluding `length`; class instances contribute own enumerable fields, excluding prototype methods. Map and Set entries and a Date's stored time are not enumerable properties, so they are not extracted. Any extra own enumerable properties on those objects are still eligible.

Pass an object as an argument, even when its properties contain primitive values:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

withDefaults({}, { count: 0 });  // => { count: 0 }
withDefaults({}, 123);           // => throws TypeError
```

#### Comparison with JavaScript defaults

The fallback rule matches JavaScript [default parameters](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Default_parameters) and [destructuring defaults](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Destructuring#default_value): only `undefined` uses an earlier value. The evaluation timing differs. JavaScript default expressions run only when needed; objects passed to `withDefaults` have already been evaluated, and the helper reads their eligible properties in argument order.

---

### `defaultsFor(defaultValues)`

Creates a reusable function that applies the same defaults to multiple objects using a shallow merge.

Pass the defaults once, then call the returned function with overrides for each object. Each call starts with the current defaults and returns a new object, so overrides from one call do not carry over to the next.

The returned function accepts zero or more override objects and follows the [withDefaults rules](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides). Overrides are applied from left to right: missing properties and `undefined` keep earlier values, while `null`, `false`, `0` and empty strings replace them. Omitting overrides makes a shallow copy of the current defaults; arguments that are `null` or `undefined` are skipped.

The defaults are kept by reference and read when the returned function is called. Changing the original defaults therefore affects future calls.

**Parameters**

| Parameter       | Type     | Description                                                                                          |
| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `defaultValues` | `object` | The defaults object to reuse. Required; must be an object other than `null`. Functions are rejected. |

**Returns:** `Function` — `(...overrides) => Object` — A reusable function that combines the current defaults with its override arguments. Each call returns a new object; nested values keep their original references.

**Errors**

- `TypeError` if `defaultValues` is missing, `null`, `undefined` or not an object, including a function. Rejected values are not stringified, coerced or invoked, including through callable-proxy traps.
- Calls to the returned function can throw the [same validation, getter and proxy errors as withDefaults](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides). Arguments are processed in order, and earlier side effects are not undone.

**Examples**

Create the function once and use it for separate objects. The second call starts with the default title, even though the first call replaced it:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultsFor } = require('go-defaults');

const applyDefaults = defaultsFor({ title: 'Home', visible: true });

applyDefaults({ title: 'About' });                     // => { title: 'About', visible: true }
applyDefaults({ visible: false });                     // => { title: 'Home', visible: false }
```

Missing override arguments, undefined properties and explicit values have different effects:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultsFor } = require('go-defaults');

const applyDefaults = defaultsFor({ title: 'Home', visible: true });

applyDefaults();                                       // => { title: 'Home', visible: true }
applyDefaults(null);                                   // => { title: 'Home', visible: true }
applyDefaults({ title: undefined, visible: false });   // => { title: 'Home', visible: false }
applyDefaults({ title: null });                        // => { title: null, visible: true }
applyDefaults({ count: 0 });                           // => { title: 'Home', visible: true, count: 0 }
```

You can also supply several override objects in one call. Here, the final undefined title preserves `'About'`:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultsFor } = require('go-defaults');

const applyDefaults = defaultsFor({ title: 'Home', visible: true });
const page = { title: 'About' };
const changes = { title: undefined, visible: false };

applyDefaults(page, null, changes);                    // => { title: 'About', visible: false }
```

**Notes**

#### Changes to the defaults

The returned function reads the original defaults on every call. Compare the results before and after editing that object:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultsFor } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { title: 'Home' };
const applyDefaults = defaultsFor(defaults);

applyDefaults();               // => { title: 'Home' }
defaults.title = 'About';
applyDefaults();               // => { title: 'About' }
```

#### Shared nested values

Each result is a new outer object, but nested objects and arrays remain shared. Changing a nested object through one result also changes the defaults and what later calls return:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultsFor } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { appearance: { colour: 'blue' } };
const applyDefaults = defaultsFor(defaults);
const firstPage = applyDefaults();

firstPage.appearance.colour = 'red';
const secondPage = applyDefaults();

defaults.appearance.colour;                      // => 'red'
secondPage.appearance.colour;                    // => 'red'
firstPage === secondPage;                        // => false
firstPage.appearance === secondPage.appearance;  // => true
```

## TypeScript

### Property inference

For ordinary objects with known properties, TypeScript infers the result from the defaults and overrides. A defined override supplies the new property type; an undefined override keeps the earlier type:

```typescript
import { withDefaults, defaultsFor } from 'go-defaults';

const preserved = withDefaults({ count: 10 }, { count: undefined });
const count: number = preserved.count;

const replaced = withDefaults({ count: 10 }, { count: 'many' });
const description: string = replaced.count;

const applyDefaults = defaultsFor({ visible: true });
const cleared = applyDefaults({ visible: null });
const visible: null = cleared.visible;
```

Inference accounts for shallow replacement, undefined fallback, optional properties, arguments that may be `null` or `undefined`, symbol keys and a fresh mutable result. Literal types supplied with `as const` stay literal types. Properties whose only possible value is `undefined` are omitted.

Numeric keys use their JavaScript string spelling, so `1` and `'1'` refer to the same property:

```typescript
import { withDefaults } from 'go-defaults';

const result = withDefaults({ 1: 'first' }, { '1': 'second' });
const byNumber: string = result[1];
const byString: string = result['1'];
```

Each property's type is calculated separately, working back from the last override until a guaranteed value is found. This avoids expanding every combination of whole-object unions, but it does not preserve relationships between different properties in a union. Narrow the source to the relevant union branch first when you need that relationship.

### When result properties are unknown

Precise inference supports tuples of up to **64 source objects**, including the defaults passed to `defaultsFor`. Larger tuples, optional or unbounded source spreads, dictionaries with index signatures, arrays and opaque `object` inputs produce a result with unknown-valued properties. This limit affects type precision; the runtime accepts any number of source objects. Complex property types remain subject to the compiler's own limits.

In a conservative result, built-in property names such as `toString`, `valueOf` and `constructor` are explicitly `unknown` too: an input may replace them with a non-function. Template-pattern index signatures, even when combined with fixed keys, use the same dictionary fallback. Finite template expansions retain their known keys.

Known native instance types, including `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, primitive wrappers, promises and binary-buffer views, also produce conservative results. Their typed methods are generally inherited and are not copied, but instances can have extra own enumerable properties. Neither the full instance type nor an empty result type would describe that reliably.

TypeScript checks structure, so an ordinary object shaped like a native wrapper—for example, one with only `valueOf(): boolean`—can also receive a conservative result. The native-type checks do not require newer ambient library definitions merely to import the package.

### Ownership and inherited properties

TypeScript does not track property ownership or enumerability. Precise inference for records assumes their visible fields are own enumerable data. For custom classes, `Error` objects, browser host objects or unusual property descriptors, widen the source to `object` to request conservative typing. This changes the inferred type, not the runtime copying rules.

Optional fields that shadow `Object.prototype` methods include the inherited fallback in their result type. For example, `{ toString?: string }` can leave either an own string or the inherited `toString` function. A guaranteed defined override retains its exact type. Host-dependent legacy prototype names such as `__proto__` remain `unknown` when every source may skip them. Undefined-only properties are still omitted from the result's own keys at runtime.

### Inputs and generic wrappers

The declarations reject known function and constructor arguments, including callable branches in unions, optional tuples and spread arrays. Function-valued properties are accepted. Broad `object` and `any` types can hide invalid arguments, so runtime validation still applies.

An unresolved generic such as `Layer extends object` can include a function intersection, even with a dictionary constraint. Passing it directly can therefore fail type checking. If a wrapper deliberately leaves validation to runtime, widen that argument to `object` and accept the conservative result type. Concrete records with generic property values retain inference; their function-valued properties remain valid.

### Compiler support

Use **TypeScript 4.5.2 or later**. The minimum applies to the compiler that checks your code, while the [runtime requirements](../README.md#runtime-support) apply to the JavaScript you run. A newer compiler can produce CommonJS code for Node.js 8; the compiler itself does not have to run on Node.js 8.

| Module resolution                                        | Minimum TypeScript version |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Traditional Node resolution (`moduleResolution: "node"`) | 4.5.2                      |
| Node16 / NodeNext                                        | 4.7.2                      |
| Bundler                                                  | 5.0.2                      |

Named imports from function subpaths require Node16, NodeNext or Bundler resolution. With legacy `node` resolution, use named root imports or default subpath imports. Default subpath imports need `esModuleInterop` for CommonJS output, or `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` for ES module output.

All three use the same inference and input-validation contracts. The package includes generated `.d.ts` declarations for older resolution modes and `.d.cts` / `.d.mts` declarations for modern CommonJS and ESM resolution.

TypeScript 4.4 and earlier are unsupported: the existing large-tuple inference cases exceed their type-recursion limits. Supporting them would require changing the declaration strategy or reducing the supported precision. The minimum preserves inference for up to 64 sources, undefined fallbacks, symbol and numeric keys, and rejection of known invalid inputs.

The compiler matrix checks 4.5.2, 4.7.2, 5.0.2, 5.4.5 and the pinned 6.0.3 compiler against an installed package. It checks supported resolution modes, optional-property settings and emitted consumers. This is a tested matrix, not a claim that every compiler patch has been run. The [development section](../README.md#development) lists the separate contributor tool requirements.
